title: Kurseong Walks and Toy Train Stations
meta_description: Six easy walks from Kurseong, to Eagle's Crag, Giddapahar, Makaibari, Dow Hill and Chimney, plus the toy train stations from Tindharia to Tung.
summary: Kurseong is the best walking base in the middle Darjeeling hills. Eagle's Crag is 15–20 minutes from the station, Makaibari 45 minutes down the Pankhabari road, Dow Hill 1–1.5 hours up and Chimney 3–3.5 hours. The toy train runs through the bazaar, with Tindharia, Gayabari and Tung nearby; services change, so check before you travel.

sections.heading: Why Kurseong suits walkers
paras: Kurseong sits at about 1,480 m on a steep ridge, with the toy train and the Hill Cart Road running through the middle of town. Within an easy walk are a viewpoint, a tea estate, a museum, an old school ridge and a forest, and most of them are linked by quiet roads rather than trails, so you need no guide and no special kit. The town is warmer than Darjeeling, which makes it pleasant to walk in from October to April, and it is small enough that you are never far from a cup of tea.

The walks below are all on roads or clear paths and suit anyone who is reasonably fit. Kurseong is steep everywhere, so every walk has a climb somewhere; plan to walk up and ride down where you can. Wear shoes with grip, carry water and a jacket, and start in the morning, because mist usually rolls in after lunch from April to September.

With two full days you can do almost everything here. Spend the first morning on Dow Hill and Chimney and the afternoon at Eagle's Crag and the bazaar. Spend the second morning walking down to Makaibari and the afternoon at the Giddapahar museum, with a jeep or taxi for the climbs back. Add a third day for the toy train or a slow drive down past Tindharia.

sections.heading: In town: Eagle's Crag and the bazaar
paras: Eagle's Crag is the short walk everyone should do. From the station, climb the lanes above the bazaar for 15–20 minutes to a small hilltop with a viewing tower. On a clear day you see down the Hill Cart Road and the ridges to the plains around Siliguri, and at night the lights of the plains spread out below. Go at sunset or early morning.

The second town walk is simply the bazaar itself, following the toy train line. The track runs down the middle of Hill Cart Road through Kurseong, with shops on both sides, and when a train is due, vendors pull back their goods and the whole street steps aside for it. Walk from the station down through the market and back, stopping for momos or tea. Walk beside the line, not on it, because trains, jeeps and people all share the same narrow space.

sections.heading: Down to Makaibari, out to Giddapahar
paras: The walk to Makaibari tea estate goes down the Pankhabari road from Kurseong bazaar, about 3–4 km and 45 minutes to an hour. The road drops through forest and then into the tea, with the estate factory and villages below. In the flush months from March to November you will see plucking on the slopes, and you can ask about a factory visit or tasting. The walk back is a steep climb of about 300 m; most people take a local jeep up for ₹20–40.

Giddapahar, about 4 km from the bazaar on the Hill Cart Road, is home to the Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose Museum, the house where Subhas Chandra Bose was held under house arrest in 1936. The walk follows the main road, so it is easy but shared with traffic; take care on the bends. Allow 45 minutes to an hour at the museum, and check opening days and timings before you travel, as they change. A taxi back to town costs about ₹300–500.

sections.heading: Up to Dow Hill and Chimney
paras: The finest walk from Kurseong climbs Dow Hill. Leave the bazaar past the post office along Dow Hill Road, and in about 1–1.5 hours you reach the ridge at roughly 1,900 m, with Victoria Boys' School, founded in 1879, and Dow Hill School among tall conifers. The forest here is the setting of Kurseong's famous ghost stories, which locals tell as folklore. The schools are closed to visitors, but the road passes their gates.

Strong walkers continue along the forest road to Chimney, about 2,200 m, where a lone 7 m brick chimney is all that survives of a dak bungalow that local accounts date to about 1839. The whole walk from Kurseong takes about 3–3.5 hours and climbs about 700 m. Stay the night in a Chimney homestay at about ₹1,200–1,800 per person with meals, or take a taxi down for ₹700–1,000. A few local jeeps also run between Bagora and Kurseong in the morning and late afternoon.

sections.heading: The toy train stations around Kurseong
paras: The Darjeeling Himalayan Railway reached Kurseong in 1880 and Darjeeling in July 1881, and UNESCO listed it as a World Heritage Site in 1999. Below Kurseong, the line climbs from the plains through Sukna and Rangtong to Tindharia, home to the railway's workshop, where its locomotives have been maintained for well over a century. Near Tindharia the line makes some of its tightest loops and zigzag reverses, including the curve known as Agony Point. Above it come Gayabari and Mahanadi, and the landslide-prone stretch at Pagla Jhora, whose name means a mad torrent, before the train reaches Kurseong.

Above Kurseong, the line climbs past Tung and Sonada to Ghoom, at 2,258 m the highest station on the line, and then drops to Darjeeling. You can see much of this from the road, since the Hill Cart Road and the track cross each other again and again. A good half day is to take a jeep down the Hill Cart Road towards Tindharia and Gayabari, watching the track, and return to Kurseong by jeep or, when it is running, by train.

sections.heading: Riding the toy train from Kurseong
paras: When the full line operates, trains run between NJP and Darjeeling via Kurseong; NJP to Kurseong takes about 5–6 hours and Kurseong to Darjeeling about 2.5–3 hours. Services on the lower section have been suspended for long periods by landslides, most famously from 2010 to 2015, and they are often cut back in the monsoon. Kurseong has sometimes been served by shorter runs to and from Darjeeling when the lower section is closed.

Book on IRCTC well ahead for October and May, when seats sell out, and choose the slowest section you can afford to spend time on: the views between Kurseong and Darjeeling, through Tung, Sonada and Ghoom, are as good as any on the line. Fares vary by class and service type, so check current status before you travel. If no train fits your dates, walking the bazaar as a train comes through and watching the line from the Hill Cart Road gives most of the experience for free.

faqs.q: What are the best walks in Kurseong?
faqs.a: The best short walk is from the station up to Eagle's Crag, 15–20 minutes, for views to the plains. Longer walks go down the Pankhabari road to Makaibari tea estate in about 45 minutes, up to the Dow Hill schools in 1–1.5 hours, and on through the forest to Chimney in 3–3.5 hours. All follow roads or clear paths.

faqs.q: How do I walk from Kurseong to Dow Hill?
faqs.a: Start in Kurseong bazaar and walk up past the post office along Dow Hill Road. It is about 3–5 km and 1–1.5 hours uphill, climbing roughly 400 m, on a road with light traffic. You reach Victoria Boys' School and Dow Hill School among tall conifers. Return the same way, take a taxi for about ₹400–600, or continue to Chimney.

faqs.q: Can I walk from Kurseong to Makaibari tea estate?
faqs.a: Yes. Walk down the Pankhabari road from Kurseong bazaar, about 3–4 km and 45 minutes to an hour, through forest and then tea gardens to the estate villages and factory. The walk back up is steep, climbing about 300 m, so most people take a local jeep up for ₹20–40 a seat or a taxi for ₹300–500.

faqs.q: Where is Eagle's Crag in Kurseong?
faqs.a: Eagle's Crag is a small hilltop viewpoint above Kurseong station, about 15–20 minutes' walk up the lanes from the bazaar. It has a viewing tower and looks down the Hill Cart Road towards the plains around Siliguri. Go at sunset or early morning for the best light. At night you can see the lights of the plains spread out below.

faqs.q: Does the toy train stop at Kurseong?
faqs.a: Yes. Kurseong is a station on the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway between NJP and Darjeeling, and the track runs through the town's bazaar. Services on the lower section have often been suspended by landslides, and shorter runs to Darjeeling have sometimes operated instead. Book on IRCTC and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is Agony Point on the toy train?
faqs.a: Agony Point is one of the tightest loops on the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway, near Tindharia below Kurseong, where the track curves so sharply that the train almost meets itself. The line also uses zigzag reverses in this area to gain height. You can see parts of these loops from the Hill Cart Road when travelling by jeep between Siliguri and Kurseong.

faqs.q: Is it safe to walk along the toy train tracks?
faqs.a: Walk beside the line, not on it. In Kurseong the track runs down the middle of the main road, shared with jeeps and pedestrians, and trains move slowly but cannot stop quickly. Outside town, the track runs along narrow ledges with steep drops. Use the Hill Cart Road or footpaths, and watch for trains, which sound their horns before bends.

faqs.q: How long does the toy train take from Kurseong to Darjeeling?
faqs.a: About 2.5–3 hours, passing Tung, Sonada and Ghoom, the highest station on the line at 2,258 m. A shared jeep covers the same 32 km in about 1–1.5 hours for ₹100–150. The train is slower but gives the classic views of the line. Schedules and fares change, so check current status on IRCTC before you travel.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide for walks around Kurseong?
faqs.a: No, for the main walks. Eagle's Crag, Makaibari, Giddapahar, Dow Hill and Chimney all follow roads or clear paths. A local guide, about ₹800–1,200 for a half day, adds value for forest birding on Dow Hill or longer walks through the tea estates, where paths branch and are not signed. Start early and return before dark.
